Lessons.Title: Analyzing Data
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: ask a statistical question; plan two comparable experimental conditions; collect and analyse authentic data; choose displays and measures of center/variability; and explain limitations. Original Edulytiks material aligned with Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 1 Lesson 16, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/1/16/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). Publisher Addressing includes HSS-ID.A and HSS-ID.A.1–A.3; Building Towards also includes HSS-ID.A.1–A.3.

Ruler-drop experiment: measure how far a dropped ruler travels before a participant catches it. Establish two test conditions, for example preferred versus non-preferred hand, keep the start point and measurement precision constant, and consider randomizing or counterbalancing the trial order. Work only with authorized voluntary participation; do not collect identity-sensitive data. Lower catch distance may suggest faster response but does not on its own prove a causal effect.

The official student task requests at least 20 observations in EACH condition. A separate first-party hypothetical dataset with only five values per condition illustrates computation and is NOT evidence that a classroom experiment occurred: A=4,6,8,10,12 centimetres, B=2,4,6,8,10 centimetres. A mean and median are 8 cm; B mean and median are 6 cm. Both MADs are (4+2+0+2+4)/5=2.4 cm; IQRs are each 6 cm under median-of-halves.

Student project: collect real observations when permitted and safe; use the source's sample-size expectation; create two comparable dot/box plots and an accessible count table; compute appropriate center and spread; and explain whether the observed results answer the statistical question. If no real experiment is possible, explicitly label a simulated analysis and seek teacher assessment of the missing physical-work requirement.

Teacher-scored rubric, 0–2 each (maximum 8): safe and comparable experimental design; correctly documented genuine observations or transparent simulation limitation; accurate displays/statistics; evidence-backed conclusion identifying confounding, measurement error and sampling limitations. Do not fabricate participants, trial counts, saved answers or physical evidence.

Source-activity A/B review, IM Algebra 1 First Edition U01:L16: Two ruler-drop conditions require 20 genuine observations EACH, if actually performed; five-value example is fictional. Keep original first-party mathematical material and graphics; source artwork identity is NOT claimed. All physical/technology/partner work remains NOT_PERFORMED unless observed.

EDULYTIKS_AUTHORED_COOLDOWN (PUBLISHER_COOLDOWN_UNVERIFIED): Compare fictional group means 8cm vs6cm and median 8cm vs6cm; five observations cannot satisfy source experiment. A teacher scores 0, 1 or 2 per criterion: Fair design and authentic n; Display and statistics; Limits and no fake participation. Total 6. KeyConcepts.Title: Two-condition experiment
KeyConcepts.Definition: A statistical investigation measures the same variable under two clearly stated conditions.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Control measurement methods and identify units and sample sizes.
KeyConcepts.Example: Preferred versus non-preferred hand with ruler-drop distance in centimetres.

KeyConcepts.Title: Comparable numerical summaries
KeyConcepts.Definition: Measures of center and spread help compare both distributions.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Display both conditions on consistent axes and apply the same statistic.
KeyConcepts.Example: In the hypothetical illustration A mean 8 cm and B mean 6 cm, both MADs 2.4 cm.

KeyConcepts.Title: Observational limitations
KeyConcepts.Definition: Confounding and measurement error constrain what may be concluded.
KeyConcepts.Rule: State how trials were conducted and do not claim a genuine experiment from synthetic numbers.
KeyConcepts.Example: Practice effects may make later ruler drops easier regardless of hand condition.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compute two hypothetical means and medians
WorkedExamples.Question: Compare A=4,6,8,10,12 cm and B=2,4,6,8,10 cm.
WorkedExamples.Method: Sort and calculate within each clearly labelled simulation group.
Steps: A total is 4+6+8+10+12=40 over five values; mean=8 cm.
Both sorted sets have the third value as median: 8 and 6.
A exceeds B by 2 cm in both centers.
The comparison is numerical only, not proof of an experiment.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Hypothetical A mean/median=8 cm, B mean/median=6 cm.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both samples contain exactly five fabricated practice observations.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare variability using MAD
WorkedExamples.Question: Find MAD of each hypothetical condition.
WorkedExamples.Method: Compute absolute distances from each condition's mean.
Steps: A absolute-deviation sum is 12, so MAD=12/5=2.4 cm.
For B mean 6, deviations are also 4,2,0,2,4.
The center differs while both samples have the same spread.
WorkedExamples.Check: B equals A minus 2 entrywise; shifting data preserves MAD.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare IQR and study requirements
WorkedExamples.Question: Find both IQRs and explain why five fabricated values cannot satisfy the source experiment.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use median-of-halves and distinguish illustration from physical data collection.
Steps: For A, lower pair 4,6 yields Q1=5; upper pair 10,12 yields Q3=11.
For B, lower pair 2,4 yields Q1=3; upper 8,10 yields Q3=9.
The source task requires at least 20 actual observations per condition; five hypothetical numbers are only a worked example.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Both IQRs equal 6 cm; actual experiment remains unperformed.
WorkedExamples.Check: Quartile calculations match the declared convention and simulated n=5 is less than required n=20.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Counting five fictional trials as actual participation
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: No physical measurements or real participants are established.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Require real documentation or label the analysis as simulation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Changing more than the intended experimental variable
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Practice effects, inconsistent drop heights or trial order confound a comparison.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep conditions comparable and counterbalance order.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a difference of means as universal causation
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Small uncontrolled samples do not establish causality.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Discuss sample size, measurement error and alternative explanations.

SummaryPoints: An experiment must define conditions, variables, units, procedure and real observations.
The official lesson asks for at least 20 ruler-drop measurements per condition; invented five-point data do not satisfy this requirement.
In the fictional arithmetic demonstration, means 8 and 6 cm differ, while MADs 2.4 and IQRs 6 cm agree.
Teacher-scored scientific reasoning and genuine sample evidence are essential; never auto-approve a fabricated physical task.
